lessons.title: The fighting debate
lessons.objective: Understand both sides of the fighting debate.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: Fighting keeps the game physical and deters cheap shots.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Fighting is a deterrent to other infractions.
options.explanation: Correct. That is the traditional argument: fights discourage players from taking liberties.

options.text: Fighting is the main point of hockey.
options.explanation: Fighting has declined sharply; most fans care far more about the skill game than fights.

options.text: Physical play is no longer allowed.
options.explanation: Hockey is still physical, but checking and hitting rules prevent dangerous play without needing fights.

payload.translation: The pro-fighting argument is that it deters other fouls and protects star players.

followUps.line: Does the PWHL have the same view on fighting?
followUps.why: Tests if you know the PWHL treats fighting differently than the NHL.

followUps.line: What is the safety-side argument against it?
followUps.why: Shows you understand the other camp values head safety over tradition.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Understanding why people value fighting doesn't mean you agree; both sides have real points.

payload.title: The safety side of the fighting debate
payload.setting: She mentions that the PWHL doesn't allow fighting.

exchanges.theirMessage: The PWHL banned fighting and it is made the game safer.

replies.text: Do the players seem to miss that part, or does the game feel fine without it?
replies.theirResponse: The game is fun. Some old-school fans miss it, but the safety is real.
replies.coachNote: You're exploring both sides; that is mature.
You agree, but do not ask or explore.

replies.theirResponse: That is one view. Some people loved that intensity.
replies.coachNote: Agreeing without exploring her point misses the real debate.

payload.closingNote: Fighting is a genuine debate: tradition and deterrence versus safety and health.

payload.prompt: The decline in NHL fighting is mostly because of stricter rule enforcement.

scene.alt: Hockey players showing reduced fighting over decades.

explanation.correct: False. The NHL still allows five-minute fighting majors. The decline is cultural: the game evolved toward valuing speed and skill, not stricter enforcement.
explanation.incorrect: Rules did not change much. Fewer fights happen because fans and players shifted priorities toward the skill game.

payload.prompt: Complete the comparison of fighting across leagues.
payload.template: The NHL still allows fights as a {{penalty-type}}, but the PWHL treats fighting as {{treatment}} and {{description}}.

explanation.correct: Right. The NHL's five-minute fighting major versus the PWHL's penalty-driven approach shows two different philosophies.
explanation.incorrect: The NHL allows five-minute majors for fights; the PWHL, being newer and skill-focused, punishes them instead.

payload.prompt: What is the core tension in the fighting debate?

options.text: Whether the NHL allows fighting at all.
Whether fighting deters infractions versus whether it risks head injuries.
Whether men's and women's hockey should have the same rules.
Who is tougher, old-school or modern players.

explanation.correct: Correct. The debate is tradition and deterrence (pro) versus safety and concussions (con). Both sides have legitimate points.
explanation.incorrect: The core disagreement is values: deterrence and toughness versus player health and injury prevention. The NHL still allows it; that is not the debate.

lessons.title: The loser point
lessons.objective: Explain why fans disagree about the loser point.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: We lost in overtime but at least got the loser point. Still, it feels weird to reward a loss.

payload.question: What is her frustration?

options.text: The loser point rewards overtime losses, which muddles the standings.
options.explanation: Correct. She is questioning why a loss should earn a point.

options.text: Overtime should not be played at all.
options.explanation: She is not saying overtime should not exist; she is questioning the point system.

options.text: Her team should have won the game.
options.explanation: That is hindsight, not her actual point about the loser point system.

payload.translation: The loser point gives a point for losing in overtime, which some fans see as rewarding failure.

followUps.line: What is the PWHL's approach to this?
followUps.why: Tests if you know the PWHL uses 3-2-1-0 instead.

followUps.line: Why do you think the NHL created the loser point?
followUps.why: Shows curiosity about the reasoning behind the rule.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The loser point is genuinely controversial; smart fans disagree on whether it helps or hurts the standings.

payload.prompt: Why was the loser point created in the NHL?

options.text: To make overtime more exciting for fans.
To reward competitive close games and discourage early-game tactics.
To simplify the standings system.
To match European hockey rules.

explanation.correct: Correct. The loser point rewards a team that was close enough to tie late, signaling competitiveness.
explanation.incorrect: The loser point rewards close losses and discourages pulling the goalie in regulation. It is meant to value competition, though some say it distorts the race.

payload.prompt: Two teams have identical point totals and the same number of regulation wins. They are tied in the standings.

scene.alt: Standings comparison of two equal teams.

explanation.correct: True. Points are all the standings show. The tiebreaker is regulation wins, then regulation plus overtime wins (ROW).
explanation.incorrect: The standings sort by points only. Other stats like overtime losses are tracked separately as tiebreakers if needed.

payload.prompt: Complete the PWHL points system.
payload.template: The PWHL uses a {{system}} point system: a regulation win is {{rw}} points, an overtime win is {{ow}} points, and a shootout loss is {{sl}} points.

explanation.correct: Right. The PWHL's 3-2-1-0 is cleaner than the NHL loser point: regulation win (3), overtime win (2), shootout loss (1), regulation loss (0).
explanation.incorrect: The PWHL uses 3-2-1-0. This avoids the NHL's loser-point confusion by separating wins and losses into clearer tiers.

lessons.title: Overtime and the shootout
lessons.objective: Explain the format debate between 3-on-3 and the shootout.

statement.speaker: Morgan
statement.text: 3-on-3 is exciting but then the shootout feels like a gimmick.

payload.question: What is her concern?

options.text: The shootout is one-on-one, not a team game like hockey.
options.explanation: Correct. She is saying the shootout is not hockey; it is a separate contest.

options.text: The shootout always decides the game fairly.
options.explanation: She thinks it is unfair, not fair.

options.text: 3-on-3 should not be played.
options.explanation: She likes 3-on-3; her issue is only with the shootout afterward.

payload.translation: The criticism of the shootout is that hockey is a team game, and one-on-one is not hockey.

followUps.line: What would you do instead of a shootout?
followUps.why: Tests if you have thought about alternatives.

followUps.line: How long can teams play 3-on-3?
followUps.why: Shows curiosity about the practical limits of overtime.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Many purists have the same view; this is a real debate, not a fringe opinion.

payload.title: The overtime format debate
payload.setting: She says her team lost in a shootout and she is frustrated.

exchanges.theirMessage: Shootout loss. I hate how one shooter decides the whole game.

replies.text: Some fans want more 3-on-3 overtime instead. Do you think they should extend it?
replies.theirResponse: Maybe, but five minutes of that is exhausting. You cannot play forever.
replies.coachNote: You are exploring the tradeoff: 3-on-3 is exciting but tiring.
You are sympathetic, but not exploring the real issue.

replies.text: The shootout is exciting. Everyone gets a chance.
replies.coachNote: Do not defend the format when she is upset about the result.

payload.closingNote: 3-on-3 is thrilling; the shootout ends the drama but feels anti-climactic to many.

payload.prompt: 3-on-3 overtime is sudden death, which means a goal always ends the game immediately.

scene.alt: Three players per side in open-ice overtime.

explanation.correct: False. 3-on-3 is sudden death only within its five-minute window. If the period ends scoreless, a shootout breaks the tie.
explanation.incorrect: 3-on-3 sudden death lasts five minutes. If neither team scores in that time, the shootout decides.

payload.prompt: How long is a standard 3-on-3 overtime period in the NHL regular season?

explanation.incorrect: Regular-season 3-on-3 is five minutes. Playoff overtime has no time limit: 20-minute periods until someone scores.

lessons.title: Analytics versus the eye test
lessons.objective: Explain both analytics and the eye test in evaluation.

statement.speaker: Casey
statement.text: The stats say he is good but I do not see it when I watch.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: A gap between what data shows and what she observes.
options.explanation: Correct. She is noting a disagreement between analytics and her eye test.

options.text: A player who is declining in ability.
options.explanation: That is one possibility, but she is really about the stat-versus-eye gap.

options.text: Stats are always wrong.
options.explanation: She is not saying stats are wrong; she is saying they disagree with her view.

payload.translation: The analytics-versus-eye-test debate: data-driven evaluation versus watching the game live.

followUps.line: What stats might he be good at that you do not notice?
followUps.why: Shows you understand stats capture things an eye test might miss.

followUps.line: Could both be right about different things?
followUps.why: Tests if you see the value in both approaches.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: This is a real debate in hockey. Smart fans use both stats and eyes.

payload.title: Analytics and the eye test
payload.setting: She follows traditional analysis and is skeptical of advanced stats.

exchanges.theirMessage: Everyone talks about Corsi now. I just watch the game.

replies.text: Corsi counts shot attempts. Do you notice when one team is dominating that count?
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, if one team is all over the other. But sometimes it does not matter.
replies.coachNote: You connected the stat to what she sees, and she is teaching you when it breaks down.

replies.text: Stats miss the real flow of the game.
replies.coachNote: You agree, but do not explore when stats are useful.

replies.theirResponse: Not always. Sometimes the better team gets out-attempted.
replies.coachNote: Do not oversell stats to someone who trusts her eyes.

payload.closingNote: Analytics and the eye test are complementary, not enemies. The best fans use both.

payload.prompt: A team has 55% Corsi but loses 2-1. What might explain this?

options.text: Their shots were lower quality or from the perimeter.
The goalie let in higher-danger shots.
Both teams' shot quality differed, or their goalie was off that night.
Corsi is meaningless.

explanation.correct: Correct. Corsi counts volume, not quality. A team can out-attempt opponents and still lose if the quality of chances is lopsided.
explanation.incorrect: Corsi shows volume of attempts, not their danger. More attempts do not guarantee more goals.

payload.prompt: Match the analytics term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: All shot attempts (shots, blocks, misses) by one team divided by both teams' attempts.
Shooting percentage plus save percentage; high PDO often indicates luck.
A probabilistic model assigning each shot a chance of scoring based on location.

explanation.summary: These stats describe effort (Corsi), luck (PDO), and quality (xG). Knowing the difference helps interpret what stats actually say.

lessons.title: Hits, discipline and player safety
lessons.objective: Explain the discipline debate and safety concerns.

statement.speaker: Taylor
statement.text: That hit was clear boarding but no suspension. The DOPS is inconsistent.

payload.question: What is her complaint?

options.text: A dangerous play did not get punished consistently.
options.explanation: Correct. She is frustrated with unpredictable DOPS decisions.

options.text: Boarding should not be a penalty.
options.explanation: She thinks boarding should be punished; she is complaining it was not.

options.text: Her team got unfairly targeted.
options.explanation: She may feel that way, but her actual complaint is about consistency.

payload.translation: Department of Player Safety decisions are hard to predict and seem inconsistent.

followUps.line: What factors do you think DOPS considers?
followUps.why: Shows curiosity about how suspensions are decided.

followUps.line: How would you make it more consistent?
followUps.why: Tests if you have thought about solutions.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Even analysts struggle to predict DOPS decisions. This is a legitimate frustration.

payload.prompt: A player takes a hit and looks dazed next shift. Assess and decide.

situation.narrative: The player took a hit in open ice; his head snapped back. Next shift he looks dazed.

facts.label: Protocol
facts.value: Immediate assessment required for visible signs.

options.label: Let him keep playing.
options.consequence: Risks serious injury. Concussions worsen if untreated.
considerations: Players do not always report symptoms.
Visible signs require immediate action.

options.label: Pull him for assessment.
options.consequence: Protects his health. Even if nothing, safety protocol is correct.
considerations: Head safety is priority over playing time.
Better to assess and return than miss a concussion.

options.label: Wait for his complaint.
options.consequence: Delays risk; concussions can worsen unseen.
considerations: Modern protocols do not wait for player-reported symptoms.
Dazed state is sufficient reason to remove.

payload.expertNote: Modern protocol pulls immediately for any sign of head impact or dazed state. Safety errs toward caution.

payload.prompt: Starting in 2026-27, all NHL players must wear neck protection.

explanation.correct: False. Neck protection is required for players with no prior NHL games. Existing players can choose.
explanation.incorrect: The rule applies to rookies and players new to the league, not veterans. This was a compromise between safety and tradition.

payload.prompt: Complete the statement about legal versus illegal hits.
payload.template: The debate centers on the line between a legal {{legal-type}} and an illegal hit to the {{target}}.

explanation.correct: Right. A legal shoulder-to-shoulder check versus a hit that targets or results in head contact is the core debate.
explanation.incorrect: Legal body contact versus illegal head contact is the boundary. Refs interpret intent and impact inconsistently.

lessons.title: When to pull the goalie
lessons.objective: Judge coaching decisions on pulling the goalie.

payload.prompt: Down by one goal with 2:30 left. Decide on the goalie.

situation.narrative: You are down a goal with 2:30 remaining in the third period.

options.label: Pull the goalie now.
options.consequence: Modern analytics favors this. Extra time increases tie chances.
considerations: Short-handed risk is real but manageable.
Extra minutes for offense outweigh the breakaway risk.

options.label: Wait until 90 seconds left.
options.consequence: Balances risk and time. Traditional approach.
considerations: Reduces breakaway exposure.
Still gives time for a chance at the net.

options.label: Keep the goalie in.
options.consequence: Wastes time without reason. Reduces tie chances.
considerations: Hoping for a miracle is not strategic.
Limits your chances to score.

payload.expertNote: Data clearly shows pulling with 2:30 is more effective than waiting. Most modern coaches pull by 3 minutes remaining.

payload.title: When should the goalie come out?
payload.setting: She disagrees with the coach keeping the goalie in late.

exchanges.theirMessage: Three minutes left down a goal and he still has the goalie in. Why wait?

replies.text: That is the modern debate. Data says pull earlier, but coaches fear the short-handed goal.
replies.theirResponse: But the tie is worth the risk, is not it?
replies.coachNote: You explained the tension; now she is engaging.

replies.text: He should pull him. That is basic.
replies.theirResponse: But they could get scored on.
replies.coachNote: You agree, but did not address her concern about risk.

replies.text: You cannot pull the goalie that early. Too risky.
replies.coachNote: Do not back tradition over what the data says works.

payload.closingNote: Pulling the goalie is about risk versus reward. More time to tie is worth more risk than one minute left.

payload.prompt: An empty-net goal counts as a regular goal on the stat sheet.

scene.alt: Puck going into an undefended net.

explanation.correct: True. Empty-netters count fully. Some fans dismiss them as cheap, but a goal is a goal.
explanation.incorrect: Empty-netters count as real goals. They are credited to the player and count in all stats. No asterisk.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: The coach pulled him too early and we gave up an empty-netter. That is why you wait.

payload.question: What is she concluding?

options.text: One bad result does not prove the strategy is wrong.
options.explanation: Correct. One game does not refute an overall strategy that works more often than not.

options.text: Early pulls always fail.
options.explanation: She had one bad outcome, but statistically early pulls work more often.

options.text: Coaches never make mistakes.
options.explanation: She is not saying the coach was right; she is using one loss to argue against a strategy.

payload.translation: One game with a bad outcome does not disprove a strategy that works on average.

followUps.line: If pulling earlier usually works, why not always do it?
followUps.why: Tests if you know there is still real risk.

followUps.line: How do coaches decide?
followUps.why: Shows curiosity about decision-making under uncertainty.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Sports involve luck. A smart decision can have a bad outcome.

lessons.title: Last change chess
lessons.objective: Read matchups and understand last change advantage.

payload.prompt: Their top line is on the ice. You have last change. Choose your matchup.

situation.narrative: The visiting team's top scoring line just took the ice. You, as the home team, have last change and see which players they sent.

facts.label: Your advantage
facts.value: You pick after seeing their players.

options.label: Send your top line; trade scoring.
options.consequence: You get an offensive matchup but miss the defensive value of last change.
considerations: Could work if you out-score them.
Wastes the defensive advantage of last change.

options.label: Send your shutdown defense.
options.consequence: Classic last change use: neutralize their stars with your best defense.
considerations: Stops their best threats.
In a tight game, defense matters more than offense.

options.label: Send whoever is fresh.
options.consequence: You waste last change's advantage by not being strategic.
considerations: No plan defeats the purpose of last change.
Random matching leaves their stars unguarded.

payload.expertNote: Last change is most valuable defensively. Sending your shutdown pair against their stars is textbook strategy.

payload.prompt: Last change matters more when a team is tied or close to tied in score.

explanation.correct: True. When the game is close, every matchup matters. When ahead or behind, line matching is secondary.
explanation.incorrect: Last change is most valuable in tight games. When protecting a big lead, matchups are less critical.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: They had last change and our top line never got going because they kept matching against our shutdown pair.

payload.question: What happened?

options.text: The home team used last change to neutralize her team's best players.
options.explanation: Correct. That is exactly what last change is designed to do.

options.text: Her top line was not good enough that night.
options.explanation: The line may have been fine; the tactic simply shut them down.

options.text: The home team was afraid of her top line.
options.explanation: Strategically matching is not fear; it is smart coaching.

payload.translation: Last change is the home team's tactic to put its best defensive pair against the opponent's best scorers.

followUps.line: What would you do if you were the visiting team?
followUps.why: Tests if you think about counter-tactics.

followUps.line: Is last change only about defense?
followUps.why: Shows you are thinking deeper about strategy.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Understanding a tactic does not mean you have to like it. Knowing how it works is the point.

options.text: The 1-3-1 relies on point shots; they did not cycle it back.
options.explanation: Correct. The formation breaks down if players do not execute the setup.

options.text: The 1-3-1 is a bad formation.
options.explanation: The formation is fine; the execution was the problem.

options.text: The defense was too strong.
options.explanation: That is possible, but she is talking about a tactical breakdown, not defense.

followUps.why: Tests if you know the purpose of the formation.

followUps.line: What would you try instead?
followUps.why: Shows you are thinking about alternatives.

payload.prompt: What does a 25% power play percentage mean?

options.text: The team scores on about one out of every four power plays.
One out of four power plays results in a shot.
The power play is used 25% of the game.
The team shoots 25% of the game's total shots on power plays.

explanation.correct: Correct. Power play percentage is goals divided by opportunities. 25% is very good.
explanation.incorrect: Power play percentage is goals scored divided by power-play chances. A 25% rate means about one goal per four opportunities.

payload.prompt: An 18% power play percentage is above average in the modern NHL.

explanation.correct: True. Around 20% is league average. 18% is close and still solid. 23%+ is elite.
explanation.incorrect: Around 20% is average. An 18% power play is below average but still respectable. Elite is 23%+.

payload.prompt: How does the NHL lottery work?

options.text: The worst team automatically gets the first pick.
A lottery drawing gives the worst teams a chance, but it is not guaranteed.
The best team that missed the playoffs gets first.
Any team can win regardless of record.

explanation.correct: Correct. The lottery gives non-playoff teams a chance, with worse records having better odds. The worst team has about a 25% chance at first overall.
explanation.incorrect: The NHL lottery reduces incentive to tank deliberately by giving non-playoff teams a chance at top picks, not guarantees.

payload.prompt: Match the draft term to its meaning.

A drawing that gives non-playoff teams a chance at top picks, reducing incentive to tank.
A young player drafted or developed but not yet a regular in the NHL.

payload.prompt: Record 10-20 in November. Season is lost. What now?

options.label: Trade veterans for picks; start the rebuild.
options.consequence: Maximize return on departing stars. Build future assets.
considerations: Get the best value while stars still have trade value.

options.consequence: Risk losing free agents with nothing in return. Sell low at deadline.

Free agents walk away in summer for nothing.
